transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Thanks for seeing me. Well, I guess what brings me in is this... this constant restless feeling I have. It’s like I’m wound too tight and I just can’t fully settle. Like, even when I’m supposed to be calmly sitting through a planning meeting at work—I’m a retail buyer, and right now we are knee-deep in the spring catalog negotiations, which is honestly exhausting because the supply chain issues are still a total mess, especially with the textiles we import. I was on the phone for two hours yesterday just trying to track down a shipment of linen blouses. 

But anyway, yeah, I just can't seem to settle down. Even when I try to do things that are supposed to be relaxing, you know? Like painting, or doing yoga. I actually just switched to a new yoga studio downtown because my old instructor moved to Portland—which is a shame, she was great, she had this beautiful rescue greyhound that used to hang out in the lobby. But even there, on the mat, I just feel completely wound up. So, yeah, I guess that's why I'm here.
How long have you been feeling this constant restlessness and difficulty settling down—days, weeks, or months?

Well, let me think. I guess it's been... really noticeably harder to manage for about two years and two months? Yeah, that sounds right, because that's right around the time the conflicts with my in-laws started taking over more of our evenings. My husband's mother, she has very strong opinions about how we should be remodeling our kitchen, which is ridiculous because she lives three states away and hasn't even seen the new countertops we picked out. We went with this beautiful quartz, kind of a grayish-white with subtle veining, because marble is just too porous, you know? You spill one glass of red wine and it's ruined forever. My sister had marble in her last house and she was constantly stressing over it. 

But anyway, yeah, the evenings just became this whole... ordeal. And ever since then, about two years and a couple of months ago, that wound-up feeling has just been there all the time. I'll be trying to chop vegetables for dinner and I just feel like I need to be doing five other things.
Over the past two years, would you say you've felt this keyed-up or restless more days than not, or does it come and go in more distinct episodes?

Oh, definitely more days than not. It's pretty much an everyday thing at this point. It doesn't really come and go, it's just sort of... always humming in the background. Like a refrigerator, you know? Actually, speaking of refrigerators, we had to replace ours last month because the ice maker completely froze up and flooded the hardwood in the kitchen. It was a disaster. We had to have these giant industrial fans blowing in there for three days straight, and the noise was just unbelievable. My husband was ready to pull his hair out, but honestly, I almost preferred the noise to the quiet? It gave me something to focus on. But anyway, we ended up getting one of those French door models, which I love, except the freezer drawer is a little sticky. I need to call the manufacturer about that. But yes, to answer your question, it's pretty much all the time, not just in episodes.
Along with this constant restlessness, have you noticed trouble falling or staying asleep, or feeling unusually tired during the day?

Sleep? No, actually, I sleep fine. I don't really have any trouble falling asleep, and I'm not unusually tired during the day. 

We did just get a new mattress, though, which might be helping? It's one of those hybrid ones—memory foam on top, but with the coils underneath. My husband insisted on it because his lower back has been bothering him so much lately. But honestly, I keep telling him his back only hurts because he absolutely refuses to hire anyone to do the yard work. He was out there for four hours on Sunday trying to pull up these old azalea bushes by the front porch. I told him to just ask our neighbor, Dave, for his landscaper's number. Dave's yard always looks immaculate. They come every Tuesday and do this perfect edging along the driveway. I actually had the number—Dave wrote it down for me on the back of a dry-cleaning receipt—but I think I accidentally tossed it when I was cleaning out my purse last week. I really need to get a purse organizer, one of those felt inserts? We're actually sourcing some of those for the fall accessories line at work, and the samples look amazing. 

But, wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, sleeping. Yeah, no, my sleep is completely fine. I'm not tired during the day or anything.
Do you notice muscle tension, like tightness in your shoulders or jaw, or trouble concentrating because your mind feels too busy?

Muscle tension? No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, my shoulders get a little sore sometimes, but that's just because I'm always lugging around these massive tote bags full of fabric swatches for work. We're sourcing for the spring collection right now, and we're doing a lot of heavy linens this year. Linen is making a huge comeback, especially in those earthy, muted tones—terracotta, sage green, that sort of thing. 

I was just telling my junior buyer that we need to push our supplier for a better margin on the terracotta because it's going to absolutely fly off the shelves. The supplier is this guy based out of Milan, super nice guy, but he takes forever to reply to emails. I swear they just take three-hour lunches over there. Which honestly sounds amazing, doesn't it? Imagine just stopping everything in the middle of the day for three hours to eat pasta and drink wine. I'd probably need a nap after that, though. I don't know how they get any work done in the afternoon. 

But wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, the jaw tightness and concentrating. No, I don't clench my jaw or anything, and my mind being busy doesn't really mess with my concentration.
Have you noticed yourself feeling more irritable or easily annoyed than usual over these past two years?

Irritable? No, not really. I mean, I don't think I'm any more easily annoyed than anyone else would be. I feel like I'm usually pretty easygoing. 

Though I will say, the one thing that does get under my skin lately is the new checkout system they installed at my local grocery store. Have you seen these things? They replaced half the regular registers with these self-checkout kiosks that are supposed to be "smart," but they just yell at you the entire time. "Unexpected item in the bagging area." Like, no, it's not unexpected, it's a lemon! I just scanned it! I was there on Tuesday trying to buy ingredients for this new chicken piccata recipe I saw on Pinterest. It looked so good in the video—they used extra capers, which I love. Capers are so underappreciated, don't you think? They add this perfect salty bite to everything. Anyway, I couldn't get the machine to scan the capers, and the little light on top started flashing red, and I had to stand there for five minutes waiting for the teenager working the front to come override it. He was just standing there texting, totally oblivious. Kids these days are just glued to their screens. My niece is like that, she's fourteen and I swear her phone is surgically attached to her hand. 

But, um, what did you ask me? Oh, irritability. Yeah, no, I don't think I've been feeling more irritable than usual over the last couple of years. Just the normal stuff.
Do you find yourself feeling easily fatigued or worn out, even after a normal amount of activity or rest?

Fatigued? Um, no, not really. I mean, I have normal energy levels, I think. I don't feel worn out after doing regular stuff. 

Actually, I usually have plenty of energy, which is good because my sister just got a new puppy and I've been helping her with it. It's a golden doodle, and oh my gosh, the energy on this dog is insane. We took him to the dog park on Saturday, and he just ran in circles for an hour straight. I don't know how he does it. The dog park is really nice, though, they just redid the fencing and put in these little agility ramps. I tried to get the puppy to go up one, but he was way more interested in chewing on a stick he found. Dogs are so funny like that, you buy them a basket full of expensive toys and they just want to play with a piece of trash. Kind of like toddlers, honestly. When my son was two, I bought him this huge wooden train set for Christmas, and he spent the entire morning playing with the cardboard box it came in. I ended up just leaving the box in the living room for a week because he loved it so much. 

But wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, feeling worn out. Right. No, I don't really feel easily fatigued or anything.

Aside from the physical restlessness, do you find yourself worrying excessively about a number of different things—like work, family, or health—and having a hard time controlling or stopping those worries?

Worrying? No, not really. I don't think I'm much of a worrier. I mean, I think about things I need to get done, but I don't sit around stressing or feeling like I can't stop thinking about them. 

I usually just tackle whatever is in front of me. Like right now, we're already planning the holiday window displays at work, which is always a massive project. We're doing this whole "winter wonderland" theme this year, but with a modern twist—lots of geometric acrylic snowflakes instead of the traditional fake snow. Fake snow is the absolute worst to clean up, by the way. We used it three years ago, and I swear I was still finding little white flecks in my shoes in July. It's just like glitter. Glitter is another one—never let a child do a craft project with glitter in your house. My son made me a Mother's Day card with red glitter when he was in kindergarten, and it somehow got permanently embedded in the grout of our kitchen tiles. I was down on my hands and knees scrubbing it with a toothbrush for hours. Do you know how hard it is to find a good grout cleaner that doesn't smell like pure bleach? I actually found this amazing citrus one at a farmer's market once, made by this lovely older couple who kept bees... 

Um, wait, sorry. What did you ask me about? Oh, worrying about health and family and stuff. Right. Yeah, no, my mind doesn't really get stuck on worries like that. I'm usually too busy just doing things to really sit around and fret.
Aside from feeling physically wound up, do you ever notice an actual feeling of nervousness, fear, or being 'on edge' inside, separate from the physical restlessness?

Nervous or on edge? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really get that internal fearful feeling, you know? It's more just... I have to keep moving. 

Like yesterday, I was at the fabric wholesaler trying to source this specific velvet for our winter display—not the crushed velvet, that looks so cheap, but a real, heavy cotton velvet. The supplier was taking forever to pull the samples, and I just couldn't stand still. I ended up organizing their entire ribbon rack while I waited. They had it sorted by color, but not by width, which makes absolutely no sense if you're actually trying to use it for packaging. I mean, who wants a one-inch grosgrain mixed in with a quarter-inch satin? It's madness. I actually used to make all my own bows for Christmas presents when the kids were little. I had this whole system with wire and double loops. My mother taught me how to do it. She used to wrap presents so beautifully they looked like they belonged in a magazine. She'd use real pine sprigs and little silver bells. We still have some of those bells, actually, I hang them on the tree every year, even though they're completely tarnished now...

Sorry, I'm rambling again. What was the question? Oh, feeling fearful or on edge. No, I don't really feel nervous inside, just... restless, I guess. Like I need to be doing something.
Does this constant sense of needing to keep moving ever get in the way of your work, relationships, or daily activities, or cause you significant distress?

Well, I suppose it does cause some issues, yeah. Like at work, my rushing around has led to some corrected purchase orders. My planning coordinator actually has to do extra reviews of my files now because I just can't sit still at my desk long enough to double-check the spreadsheets. Just last week, I accidentally ordered 500 yards of that velvet instead of 50. Can you imagine? Where would we even store 500 yards of fabric? Our stockroom is already a complete disaster zone with all the holiday shipments coming in. We got this massive crate of glass ornaments from Germany yesterday, and the packaging was just ridiculous. They used this weird shredded wood stuff instead of bubble wrap. It gets absolutely everywhere! I had to sweep the loading dock three times. Sweeping is actually kind of nice though, it's a good way to keep moving when you're stuck in the back room. I actually bought a new broom for the house recently because the one we had... 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, getting in the way of things. Right. So work is a bit frustrating with the extra reviews. And at home... well, family dinners can get pretty tense. I guess because I'm so wound up, I tend to jump in constantly, and people feel like they're being talked over. My husband made this beautiful roast chicken on Sunday, with those little fingerling potatoes—I love those, especially when they get really crispy on the bottom of the roasting pan. You really have to use duck fat to get them perfectly crisp. I found this gourmet butcher shop downtown that sells it in little glass jars. The guy who runs it is so funny, he wears this classic striped apron and always gives me recipes... 

Anyway, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Just talking and talking. But yes, I guess the constant moving and rushing does cause some friction at work and makes dinners a bit stressful.
Thinking back to your childhood and school years, did you notice similar patterns of restlessness, difficulty staying still, or being easily distracted before adulthood?

Oh, childhood? Yeah, it was definitely there back then too. I remember in elementary school, my parents were always getting notes sent home from my teachers. It was always the same thing—I kept popping out of my seat, I was constantly talking over the other kids, and I'd just blurt out answers before the teacher even finished asking the question. 

I was just always in a rush. Like, why wait for the end of the sentence when I already knew the answer, right? I used to love reading ahead in the textbooks. Especially the history ones. I had this one teacher in fourth grade, Mrs. Gable, and she had this amazing collection of historical maps. She'd let us look at them if we finished our work early. I was obsessed with this one map of the Oregon Trail. Did you know they used to have to grease the wagon wheels with animal fat? It's wild to think about. I actually dragged my family to a pioneer museum a few years ago on a road trip. The kids hated it, but I thought it was fascinating. They had this whole interactive exhibit on churning your own butter. It takes forever! I tried it for five minutes and my arm was completely exhausted. I can't imagine doing that every single day just to have butter for your toast. I mean, now you just go to the store and buy Kerrygold. Have you tried Kerrygold? It's Irish butter, and it completely ruins you for any other kind of butter. It's so yellow and rich... 

Oh, right, the notes sent home. Yeah, I was definitely a handful in school. Always moving, always talking. So, yes, it's been like this for a long time.

patient.answer:
Irritable? No, not really. I mean, I don't think I'm any more easily annoyed than anyone else would be. I feel like I'm usually pretty easygoing. 

Though I will say, the one thing that does get under my skin lately is the new checkout system they installed at my local grocery store. Have you seen these things? They replaced half the regular registers with these self-checkout kiosks that are supposed to be "smart," but they just yell at you the entire time. "Unexpected item in the bagging area." Like, no, it's not unexpected, it's a lemon! I just scanned it! I was there on Tuesday trying to buy ingredients for this new chicken piccata recipe I saw on Pinterest. It looked so good in the video—they used extra capers, which I love. Capers are so underappreciated, don't you think? They add this perfect salty bite to everything. Anyway, I couldn't get the machine to scan the capers, and the little light on top started flashing red, and I had to stand there for five minutes waiting for the teenager working the front to come override it. He was just standing there texting, totally oblivious. Kids these days are just glued to their screens. My niece is like that, she's fourteen and I swear her phone is surgically attached to her hand. 

But, um, what did you ask me? Oh, irritability. Yeah, no, I don't think I've been feeling more irritable than usual over the last couple of years. Just the normal stuff.

inference.note: Patient denies sleep disturbance, muscle tension, and irritability, leaving only restlessness endorsed—insufficient associated symptoms (need ≥3) to meet full GAD criteria, so F41.1 is less supported; F41.9 remains as the anxiety disorder not otherwise meeting specific criteria.

doctor.intent: Assess for the remaining GAD symptom criterion (fatigue/being easily fatigued) to help meet the required number of associated symptoms for GAD diagnosis
doctor.question: Do you find yourself feeling easily fatigued or worn out, even after a normal amount of activity or rest?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling easily fatigued or worn out, which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Fatigued? Um, no, not really. I mean, I have normal energy levels, I think. I don't feel worn out after doing regular stuff. 

Actually, I usually have plenty of energy, which is good because my sister just got a new puppy and I've been helping her with it. It's a golden doodle, and oh my gosh, the energy on this dog is insane. We took him to the dog park on Saturday, and he just ran in circles for an hour straight. I don't know how he does it. The dog park is really nice, though, they just redid the fencing and put in these little agility ramps. I tried to get the puppy to go up one, but he was way more interested in chewing on a stick he found. Dogs are so funny like that, you buy them a basket full of expensive toys and they just want to play with a piece of trash. Kind of like toddlers, honestly. When my son was two, I bought him this huge wooden train set for Christmas, and he spent the entire morning playing with the cardboard box it came in. I ended up just leaving the box in the living room for a week because he loved it so much. 

But wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, feeling worn out. Right. No, I don't really feel easily fatigued or anything.

inference.note: Patient endorses chronic (2+ years) restlessness more days than not, but denies sleep disturbance, muscle tension, irritability, and fatigue, so only 1 of 6 GAD-associated symptoms (restlessness) is confirmed. This makes full GAD (F41.1) criteria not yet met, but it remains a differential pending further exploration of concentration/other symptoms; unspecified anxiety (F41.9) remains likely given prominent tangential, circumstantial speech pattern possibly reflecting anxious rumination rather than classic GAD symptom cluster.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient experiences excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple everyday issues, which is the core feature needed to distinguish Generalized Anxiety Disorder from unspecified anxiety.
doctor.question: Aside from the physical restlessness, do you find yourself worrying excessively about a number of different things—like work, family, or health—and having a hard time controlling or stopping those worries?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry and difficulty controlling those worries, which are symptoms of Generalized Anxiety Disorder. My symptom profile does not include excessive worrying.

patient.answer:
Worrying? No, not really. I don't think I'm much of a worrier. I mean, I think about things I need to get done, but I don't sit around stressing or feeling like I can't stop thinking about them. 

I usually just tackle whatever is in front of me. Like right now, we're already planning the holiday window displays at work, which is always a massive project. We're doing this whole "winter wonderland" theme this year, but with a modern twist—lots of geometric acrylic snowflakes instead of the traditional fake snow. Fake snow is the absolute worst to clean up, by the way. We used it three years ago, and I swear I was still finding little white flecks in my shoes in July. It's just like glitter. Glitter is another one—never let a child do a craft project with glitter in your house. My son made me a Mother's Day card with red glitter when he was in kindergarten, and it somehow got permanently embedded in the grout of our kitchen tiles. I was down on my hands and knees scrubbing it with a toothbrush for hours. Do you know how hard it is to find a good grout cleaner that doesn't smell like pure bleach? I actually found this amazing citrus one at a farmer's market once, made by this lovely older couple who kept bees... 

Um, wait, sorry. What did you ask me about? Oh, worrying about health and family and stuff. Right. Yeah, no, my mind doesn't really get stuck on worries like that. I'm usually too busy just doing things to really sit around and fret.

inference.note: Patient denies fatigue, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, and excessive worry, leaving only chronic restlessness. This is insufficient to meet full GAD (F41.1) criteria requiring at least 3 associated symptoms, so F41.1 is now ruled out, leaving unspecified anxiety disorder as the primary candidate pending further exploration of other symptom domains (e.g., panic attacks, medical causes).

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is accompanied by a subjective feeling of nervousness, fear, or being 'on edge,' which is a core feature of an anxiety disorder as opposed to purely physical restlessness or another cause.
doctor.question: Aside from feeling physically wound up, do you ever notice an actual feeling of nervousness, fear, or being 'on edge' inside, separate from the physical restlessness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of nervousness, fear, or being 'on edge' (symptoms of anxiety), which are not covered by my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Nervous or on edge? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really get that internal fearful feeling, you know? It's more just... I have to keep moving. 

Like yesterday, I was at the fabric wholesaler trying to source this specific velvet for our winter display—not the crushed velvet, that looks so cheap, but a real, heavy cotton velvet. The supplier was taking forever to pull the samples, and I just couldn't stand still. I ended up organizing their entire ribbon rack while I waited. They had it sorted by color, but not by width, which makes absolutely no sense if you're actually trying to use it for packaging. I mean, who wants a one-inch grosgrain mixed in with a quarter-inch satin? It's madness. I actually used to make all my own bows for Christmas presents when the kids were little. I had this whole system with wire and double loops. My mother taught me how to do it. She used to wrap presents so beautifully they looked like they belonged in a magazine. She'd use real pine sprigs and little silver bells. We still have some of those bells, actually, I hang them on the tree every year, even though they're completely tarnished now...

Sorry, I'm rambling again. What was the question? Oh, feeling fearful or on edge. No, I don't really feel nervous inside, just... restless, I guess. Like I need to be doing something.

inference.note: Patient continues to deny worry, fear, irritability, fatigue, sleep disturbance, concentration difficulty, and muscle tension, leaving only physical restlessness/need to keep moving. This is insufficient to meet full GAD (F41.1) criteria, so unspecified anxiety disorder remains the most fitting code; no new diagnoses are supported.

doctor.intent: Assess whether this restlessness causes clinically significant distress or impairment in daily functioning, which is necessary to justify an anxiety disorder diagnosis despite the absence of typical worry, tension, or fatigue.
doctor.question: Does this constant sense of needing to keep moving ever get in the way of your work, relationships, or daily activities, or cause you significant distress?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work it has led to corrected purchase orders and extra review from my planning coordinator, and at home it has made family dinners more tense because people feel talked over.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms interfere with work, relationships, or daily activities, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose it does cause some issues, yeah. Like at work, my rushing around has led to some corrected purchase orders. My planning coordinator actually has to do extra reviews of my files now because I just can't sit still at my desk long enough to double-check the spreadsheets. Just last week, I accidentally ordered 500 yards of that velvet instead of 50. Can you imagine? Where would we even store 500 yards of fabric? Our stockroom is already a complete disaster zone with all the holiday shipments coming in. We got this massive crate of glass ornaments from Germany yesterday, and the packaging was just ridiculous. They used this weird shredded wood stuff instead of bubble wrap. It gets absolutely everywhere! I had to sweep the loading dock three times. Sweeping is actually kind of nice though, it's a good way to keep moving when you're stuck in the back room. I actually bought a new broom for the house recently because the one we had... 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, getting in the way of things. Right. So work is a bit frustrating with the extra reviews. And at home... well, family dinners can get pretty tense. I guess because I'm so wound up, I tend to jump in constantly, and people feel like they're being talked over. My husband made this beautiful roast chicken on Sunday, with those little fingerling potatoes—I love those, especially when they get really crispy on the bottom of the roasting pan. You really have to use duck fat to get them perfectly crisp. I found this gourmet butcher shop downtown that sells it in little glass jars. The guy who runs it is so funny, he wears this classic striped apron and always gives me recipes... 

Anyway, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Just talking and talking. But yes, I guess the constant moving and rushing does cause some friction at work and makes dinners a bit stressful.

inference.note: Patient denies core anxiety features (subjective worry, fear, nervousness, muscle tension, fatigue, sleep disturbance) despite chronic restlessness, which weakens support for GAD. The pattern of restlessness, distractibility, tangential/pressured speech, impulsivity (ordering errors), and difficulty staying on task raises suspicion for adult ADHD, added as a differential; GAD retained but less likely.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness, distractibility, and impulsivity have been present since childhood (a key criterion for ADHD versus an adult-onset anxiety disorder)
doctor.question: Thinking back to your childhood and school years, did you notice similar patterns of restlessness, difficulty staying still, or being easily distracted before adulthood?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I remember in elementary school getting notes sent home because I kept popping out of my seat, talking over classmates, and rushing to answer before the teacher finished the question.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the presence of symptoms during childhood/school years, which corresponds to the requirement of symptom onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Oh, childhood? Yeah, it was definitely there back then too. I remember in elementary school, my parents were always getting notes sent home from my teachers. It was always the same thing—I kept popping out of my seat, I was constantly talking over the other kids, and I'd just blurt out answers before the teacher even finished asking the question. 

I was just always in a rush. Like, why wait for the end of the sentence when I already knew the answer, right? I used to love reading ahead in the textbooks. Especially the history ones. I had this one teacher in fourth grade, Mrs. Gable, and she had this amazing collection of historical maps. She'd let us look at them if we finished our work early. I was obsessed with this one map of the Oregon Trail. Did you know they used to have to grease the wagon wheels with animal fat? It's wild to think about. I actually dragged my family to a pioneer museum a few years ago on a road trip. The kids hated it, but I thought it was fascinating. They had this whole interactive exhibit on churning your own butter. It takes forever! I tried it for five minutes and my arm was completely exhausted. I can't imagine doing that every single day just to have butter for your toast. I mean, now you just go to the store and buy Kerrygold. Have you tried Kerrygold? It's Irish butter, and it completely ruins you for any other kind of butter. It's so yellow and rich... 

Oh, right, the notes sent home. Yeah, I was definitely a handful in school. Always moving, always talking. So, yes, it's been like this for a long time.

inference.note: Childhood-onset history of restlessness, blurting answers, interrupting, and inattention with functional impairment (work errors, family friction) supports ADHD. Absence of excessive worry, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, fatigue, or subjective fear/anxiety argues against GAD, so F41.9 is ruled out.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports chronic, pervasive restlessness and inner drive to keep moving present for years and traced back to childhood (school notes for out-of-seat behavior, blurting answers, interrupting peers), consistent with childhood-onset ADHD. Current presentation includes impulsivity (ordering 500 yards instead of 50), inattention (errors requiring extra review, tangential/distractible speech, losing track of conversation repeatedly), and hyperactivity (inability to sit still, needing to keep moving, organizing shelves while waiting). Functional impairment is present at work (order errors, extra oversight needed) and at home (interrupting family dinners). Classic GAD symptoms (excessive uncontrollable worry, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, fatigue, subjective nervousness) were explicitly denied, arguing against F41.1. The chronic non-episodic course and childhood onset support a neurodevelopmental disorder (ADHD) over an anxiety disorder or bipolar spectrum condition, and no discrete mood episodes were reported.
